name: Greyish Blue
lede: Greyish blue is a blue dulled with grey: the name Patrick Syme gave in 1821 to a mineralogist's smalt blue, later the color French soldiers wore into 1915, and the quiet blue of harbor skies.

sections.title: A blue with grey in it
sections.body:
Greyish blue is a plain compound, and plain compounds are loose by nature. Pastoureau separates the basic color words from a third group of shades made by joining two terms, such as grey-blue, and notes that these carry no symbolism, only an aesthetic meaning, and that their identity is vaguer [10]. Paterson's dictionary shows the looseness at work: a dozen older color names, from azulin and blunket to lead-blue, saxe blue and Payne's grey, are each defined as a greyish blue [9].

The swatch is #8AA1A6, a pale blue with almost no chroma: 9 on the CIELCH scale, so low that the nearest learnable name in our set is [[grey]], 9 units away [12]. Our library carries the name from Werner, ISCC-NBS 1955, Maerz and Paul, Ridgway, Wikipedia's color lists and the xkcd color survey [12]. The survey's own greyish blue, #5E819D, is a darker and bluer color [12]. The nearest names to our swatch are Tourmaline and Ridgway's Clear Green-Blue Grey, both about 1.5 units away [12].

sections.title: Werner's smalt blue
sections.body:
The name comes from mineralogy. In 1774 the German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner devised a list of 54 colors for identifying minerals and assembled a specimen for each [1]. He revised and expanded the list over the next forty years or so [1].

Patrick Syme (1774-1845), a flower painter in Edinburgh, published *Werner's Nomenclature of Colours* in 1814 and a second edition in 1821, with examples from animals, plants and minerals [2]. Darwin took the 1821 edition on the Beagle, and the color terms in his animal notes come from it [11].

In the 1821 edition Syme renamed two of Werner's blues [3]. His Sky Blue became Greenish Blue, number 33, and Smalt Blue became Greyish Blue, number 34 [3]. For number 34 he gave three examples: the back feathers of the blue tit, the small fennel flower, and an iron ore called iron earth [4]. His description of the color is [[berlin-blue]] with white, a little grey and a hardly noticeable trace of red [4].

sections.title: The pigment behind the name
sections.body:
Smalt is blue glass colored with cobalt. The hot glass is plunged into water, where it cracks into fragments that can be ground into pigment [5]. Its origin is obscure: tradition credits a Bohemian glassmaker, Christoph Schürer, between 1540 and 1560, but smalt already appears in Dieric Bouts's *Entombment* of about 1455 [5]. The invention has been credited instead to Italian glassmakers of the fourteenth century, and Ball also raises a Near Eastern origin [5].

Smalt had to be left coarse to keep its deep color, which made it gritty to paint with, and its luster fades in oil [5]. [[painter:titian|Titian]], Tintoretto, Veronese, [[painter:el-greco|El Greco]] and [[painter:anthony-van-dyck|van Dyck]] all used it [5]. Ball describes the sky above van Dyck's portrait of Charles I as mostly greyish-blue smalt and white, and adds that the smalt is probably discolored [6]. A greyish blue in an old painting may therefore be a plain tint or a blue that has changed.

The same grey-blue turns up at the expensive end of the market. Simple grinding of ordinary [[gem:lapis-lazuli|lapis lazuli]] gives only a greyish blue powder, and a better extraction method that freed the pure blue mineral lazurite appeared soon after 1200 [7].

sections.title: Horizon blue
sections.body:
In August 1914 French soldiers went to war in red trousers dyed with madder, and Pastoureau judges it likely that so bright a color cost tens of thousands of lives [8]. That December the army decided to replace the red with a dull, unobtrusive greyish blue [8]. The synthetic indigo needed to dye so much cloth took months to find, and only in spring 1915 were all French troops dressed in the new color, called horizon blue [8].

Other armies had already moved on. Pastoureau lists khaki for the British, greyish green for Germans, Italians and Russians, and greyish blue for the Austro-Hungarians [8]. As late as 1911 a former French war minister, Étienne, argued that dull, faded shades went against French taste and that the red trousers were France [8].

Books disagree on what the color was. Paterson lists poilu-blue as the shade of greyish blue worn by French infantrymen in the First World War, but defines horizon blue as a light greenish blue [9]. Pastoureau calls it the indefinable color of the line between sky and earth or sea [8]. He adds an older echo: peasants of the feudal period wore a dull greyish blue, and country people in England, Germany and northern Italy took to blue clothes again in the later eighteenth century [8].

sections.title: Older names for the same grey
sections.body:
Paterson defines a dozen older color names as a greyish blue: azulin, blunket, plunket, gobelin blue, lead-blue, saxe blue, Tyrian blue, a pale Botticelli blue and [[payne-s-grey]], among others [9]. Grulla is the grey-blue of some horses [9]. Venet, short for the Latin for Venice blue, is turquoise and sometimes greyish blue, and Paterson passes on a report from Maerz and Paul that spy ships used it on their sails in the fifteenth century as camouflage [9]. His [[steel-blue]] is a greenish or greyish blue, and also another name for Prussian blue [9].

The list shows what the phrase is for. Each older name pins the same region of color to a material, a place or a person, and greyish blue is the label that covers them all [9].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 416 works, 1.75 per cent [13]. It belongs to harbors and skies. [[painter:eugene-boudin|Boudin]] carries it in 9 of his 33 paintings here, about 16 times the archive rate, [[painter:alfred-sisley|Sisley]] in 7 of 50, and [[painter:childe-hassam|Hassam]] in 3 of 13 [13]. [[look:impressionism|Impressionism]] has it 6.5 times as often as the archive average, 16 of 140 paintings [13].

The canvases where it covers the most are [[painting:cma-163797|an Indian court painting of an elephant]] from 1761 at 56 per cent, [[painting:rijks-200742047|a seascape by Bakhuysen]] from 1667 and [[painting:smk-KMS3630|Guardi's *Bucintoro Festival*]], both at 52 per cent, and Boudin's [[painting:commons-Q17496120|*Voiliers*]] at 46 per cent [13]. The peak decade is the 1870s, with 43 of 1,065 paintings, 2.3 times the archive rate [13]. The first dated example is Petrus Christus's *Nativity* of 1450, and none of the 443 works from before 1400 carries it [13]. Where it appears it is usually among the lightest colors of the painting, in 69 per cent of cases [13]. It most often shares a canvas with sky blue, 13 times the usual rate, and then grey [13].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test, and a smalt sky that has discolored will read differently from the day it was painted [13][6]. In Google Books the phrase *greyish blue* stands highest in the earliest decades measured, around 1800, and has fallen to about 13 per cent of that level by 2000 [14]. To see it, look at the sky and water of a Boudin harbor: the grey in the blue is the point [13].

questions.q: What did Syme's 1821 edition do to Werner's Smalt Blue?
Why did the French army replace its red trousers with a dull greyish blue in 1914-15?
choices: The bright red was too easy to see on the battlefield
Blue was the color of the Republic's flag only
Greyish blue was cheaper than madder
questions.answer: The bright red was too easy to see on the battlefield

questions.q: Ordinary lapis lazuli, ground and washed, gives a brilliant blue powder.

openers: Syme's 1821 list renamed Werner's smalt blue as Greyish Blue, number 34, and matched it to a blue tit's back.
In spring 1915 the whole French army changed from red trousers to a dull greyish blue called horizon blue.
Look for greyish blue in harbor skies: more than a quarter of Boudin's paintings in our archive carry it.

issues: Paterson's horizon blue (light greenish blue) vs Pastoureau's grayish-blue 1915 uniform: stated as books disagree.
Smalt origin: tradition (Schurer 1540-60) vs Bouts c. 1455: stated as disputed.
Venet camouflage anecdote is Paterson relaying Maerz & Paul: hedged.
Archive matches are colors, not pigment identifications (said in text).
Checker pass: key claims re-traced to fact cards and book text; no changes needed.
